spots.name: Sagrada Família
spots.label: Sagrada Família

text.directions_text: Take Metro line L5 or Metro line L2 to Sagrada Família Metro station, which is about 1 minute on foot from the basilica, with the basilica to the south of the station. If you are coming by tram, tram T4 stops at Sicília, about 6 minutes on foot from the basilica, which lies to the north of the stop. Tram T4 also stops at Monumental Metro station (also on Metro line L2), about 9 minutes on foot from the basilica, which lies to the north-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the surrounding streets.
text.description:
The Sagrada Família is the great basilica designed by Antoni Gaudí in Barcelona's Eixample district. Building began in 1882, and Gaudí took over the design the following year and gave it his own mix of Gothic and flowing Art Nouveau forms. He worked on it for the rest of his life and is buried in the crypt. When he died in 1926 it was far from finished, and work has carried on ever since. The central Tower of Jesus Christ is 172.5 m high, which makes this the tallest church in the world. Parts of the building, including the Nativity façade and the Crypt, are part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing for Gaudí's works.

It photographs well because nothing else looks like it. Dozens of carved spires, textured stonework and sculpted detail give your phone plenty to work with, even in a quick snap. The sheer height is the main challenge, so decide early whether you want the whole building or just a detail. That can look dramatic, but if you want straighter lines, step back and keep the phone level. Expect other visitors in the frame, so be patient and shoot in the gaps.
text.geographic_location: The Sagrada Família stands in the Eixample district of Barcelona. Sagrada Família Metro station is right beside it.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sky does not wash out the detail. If you want the full height in one frame, try panorama mode held vertically, moving slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaça de Gaudí (far end of the reflecting pond, opposite the Nativity façade). The Nativity façade and its towers rising above the pond, mirrored in the water when the surface is calm. If you want the whole building in one shot, walk a little further back from this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the vertical lines of the towers straight. Hold the phone as level as you can rather than tilting it far upwards. Look for a foreground element, such as people or a tree, to give the huge building some scale. For a close-up, fill the frame with the stone carving rather than trying to include everything.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit more of the towers into the frame from close up. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the façade. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out spires and carved details high above you.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually gives softer light and fewer people in your shots. Around midday the sun is high and the light can be harsh on the stone.

spots.name: Park Güell
spots.label: Park Güell

text.directions_text: The nearest stations are on Metro line L3. Vallcarca Metro station is about 716 m from the park, which is about 12 minutes on foot, and the park lies to the east of it. Lesseps Metro station is about 886 m away, which is about 14 minutes on foot, and the park lies to the north of it. The park sits on a hillside, so allow a little extra time. Once there, follow the park paths to the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is about 60 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.access_note: The main Monumental Zone (terrace, mosaics, viaducts and gate area) needs a ticket, which often sells out, so check the official site before you go.
text.description: Park Güell is a hillside garden complex designed by Antoni Gaudí for the industrialist Eusebi Güell. It sits on the southern slope of the Turó del Carmel, so the city spreads out below it. It was meant to be a private estate of sixty villa plots, but only two houses were built. It opened to the public as a park in 1926 and is now a municipal garden. It is also part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing for Gaudí's works. It photographs well because almost everything is curved or colourful: the two gatehouses at the entrance, the long wavy bench around the main terrace, and the mosaic-covered vaulted space beneath it. The raised stone walkways have columns that look like tree trunks, which makes good leading lines. For the widest view, climb to the hill of the three crosses at the top, where the Sagrada Família, Torre Glòries, Montjuïc and the sea can be seen. Expect other visitors in most shots, so shoot a little higher or tighter to keep people out of the frame, or let them add a sense of scale. Keep your phone's lens clean, as you will be handling it a lot on the stairs and terraces. The main area has a ticket system and tickets often sell out, so book ahead where you can.
text.geographic_location: Park Güell is in the La Salut neighbourhood of Barcelona's Gràcia district, on the southern slope of the Turó del Carmel hill, at about 41.4136° N, 2.1528° E. It is a large site, around 854 m across, and it looks over the city from above the streets of Gràcia.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mosaics to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the bright tiles and sky do not wash out. If the sun is behind you, check the screen for your own shadow before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 60 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Take a few steps either way along the path to get a clean line of sight without other visitors in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use the curve of the bench or a walkway as a line leading into the frame. Include a bit of sky and city beyond the terrace edge to show the hillside setting. Keep the phone level so the architecture does not look tilted.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the terrace, the bench and the gatehouses. Use the default lens (1x) for natural-looking views of the walkways and columns. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for mosaic details and for distant views of the city.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Midday is often harsh and busy.

spots.name: Barcelona Cathedral
spots.label: Cathedral

text.directions_text: Take Metro line L4 to Jaume I Metro station, which is 194 m from the cathedral, about 3 minutes on foot, and walk west towards it. Liceu Metro station (Metro line L3) is also nearby: the cathedral is 392 m to the north-east of it, about 6 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: The cathedral is a working place of worship and visiting inside may be ticketed or restricted at times, so check the official site before you go.
text.description: Barcelona Cathedral, properly the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and Saint Eulalia, is the seat of the archbishop of Barcelona and the centrepiece of the old Gothic Quarter. The present building was begun on 1 May 1298 and took about 150 years, with the cloister finished in 1448. The tall neo-Gothic façade that many visitors picture was added later and completed in 1913, so the front looks younger than the sides. It photographs well because the towers, pointed pinnacles and carved gargoyles give you plenty of detail, and the stone looks different in every kind of light. The sources give the bell towers as 54 metres high, with the tallest point, the central lantern tower (cimborio), reaching 70 metres. Inside the cloister, 13 white geese are kept, one for each year of Saint Eulalia's life according to tradition. That is a charming small subject if you go in. From here you see the eastern end of the building rather than the façade. The streets around are narrow, so you will probably be tilting your phone upwards, and the cathedral will not fit in one shot unless you step back. Take a wide view first, then move to closer shots of the stonework and sculpture. Expect other visitors to wander through your frame, so be patient and take a few shots. Right next to it: Gothic Quarter and the Bishop's Bridge.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral stands in the Gothic Quarter (Barri Gòtic) in Barcelona's old town, a short walk from Jaume I Metro station.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the sky does not turn white. When you tilt the phone up, the lines will lean inwards, so hold it as level as you can and step back rather than tilt more.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Pla de la Seu (centre of the square, facing the main west façade). The cathedral's main façade and doorway filling the frame, the classic full-cathedral postcard shot. If the view is blocked by people, move a few steps sideways rather than closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the towers upright against the vertical lines. Leave a little sky above the highest point so the central lantern tower is not cut off. Take one wide shot, then one zoomed-in shot of the sculpture and stonework as a detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole view. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are squeezed into a narrow street and cannot fit the towers in. Use the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the gargoyles, pinnacles and stone carving higher up.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is likely to be best from the east, as the sun should be behind you and light the stone. Early or late in the day, there are usually fewer people.
